previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: The patient, a morbidly obese male with a history of ankylosing spondylitis, hypertension, asthma, obstructive sleep apnea, and anxiety, was admitted for persistent right hip pain following a recent hospitalization. He had worsening pain despite high-dose prednisone and experienced a fall due to gait instability. Evaluation revealed no signs of septic joint, with normal CRP and negative joint fluid analysis. He underwent fluoroscopic-guided right hip joint aspiration and steroid injection, which improved his pain. Hyperkalemia was identified and treated, likely due to dietary potassium salt use. His condition stabilized with pain management, IV steroids, and physical therapy. He was discharged home ambulatory with a walker, on a prednisone taper, home medications, and plans to follow up with rheumatology to discuss starting Apremilast.

PROCEDURE:  The risks, benefits, and alternatives were explained to the

A pre-procedure timeout confirmed three patient identifiers.

Under fluoroscopic guidance, an appropriate spot was marked. The area was
prepared and draped in standard sterile fashion.

5 cc 1% Lidocaine was used to achieve local anesthesia. Under intermittent

for fluid analysis and culture.

The needle was removed, hemostasis achieved, and a sterile bandage applied.

The patient tolerated the procedure well and left the department in stable
condition. There were no immediate complications or complaints.

PROCEDURE:  The risks, benefits, and alternatives were explained to the
patient and written informed consent obtained.

A pre-procedure timeout confirmed three patient identifiers.

Under fluoroscopic guidance, an appropriate spot was marked. The area was
prepared and draped in standard sterile fashion.

3 cc 1% Lidocaine was used to achieve local anesthesia. Under intermittent
fluoroscopic guidance, a 20-gauge spinal needle was advanced into the left  
hip joint. Appropriate position was confirmed by the injection of a small
amount of water soluble contrast.  A mixture of 5 cc of 0.25% Bupivacaine and
2 cc of Kenalog (80 mg total) was injected, dispersing the contrast.

The needle was removed, hemostasis achieved, and a sterile bandage applied. 
The patient experienced no significant change in symptoms immediately
following the procedure.

The patient tolerated the procedure well and left the department in stable
condition. There were no immediate complications or complaints.

FINDINGS: 

Contrast is seen within the left hip joint.

IMPRESSION: 

Technically successful therapeutic injection into the left hip joint.
